# What classical solvers do that surrogates do not {#sec-classical-solvers}

**Classical PDE and CFD solvers generalize to new geometries and conditions
because almost nothing in them is fitted to a geometry: the physics enters as
a local operator, the geometry enters as a mesh and a set of boundary
conditions, and the global coupling is produced at run time by iteration and
by exact algebra.** A learned surrogate inverts every one of those choices at
once: it fits the global map on a family, encodes geometry implicitly, and
produces the answer in one pass. The audit's four directions are each an
attempt to hand one solver ingredient back to mathematics. This chapter lists
the ingredients, states what each buys and what it costs, and derives from
each a hypothesis that an experiment in this program can reject. Papers cited
in the audit's two literature dossiers are referenced by name; the mechanism
claims here are classical numerical analysis, not new results.

## The inventory {#sec-classical-inventory}

| Ingredient of a classical solver | Why it generalizes | What it costs | What the surrogate does instead |
|---|---|---|---|
| Local discrete operator (finite volume / element stencils) | The same few-point relation holds at every cell of every mesh; geometry enters only through cell metrics | A sparse system whose solve is the whole cost | Fits a global input→output map on one family; the operator is implicit and family-specific |
| Iterative solve with a residual | Convergence is monitored against the equation, so a new geometry is solved to the same tolerance as a familiar one | Tens to thousands of operator applications | One pass; no residual, no stopping criterion, error unknown until compared to a label |
| Multigrid / coarse spaces | Smooth error is corrected on a coarse representation that exists for any geometry; the slow space is generic smoothness | Hierarchy construction; a few percent of a solve | Fixed latent size chosen by validation error; the interior spectrum is whatever training produced (@sec-solver-spaces shows source-fitted spaces lose to a free coarse grid) |
| Domain decomposition and static condensation | Local solves plus a small exact interface system; a component's response is reusable in any assembly with compatible interfaces | Interface solve; coarse space for scalability | Whole-shape regression; a new arrangement of familiar parts is a new shape |
| Boundary integral methods | The free-space kernel is universal; geometry enters through a dense but well-understood boundary operator | Dense or fast-multipole-accelerated boundary solve; only for linear homogeneous operators | Learns kernel and inverse together, on a family; the repository's exact-kernel branch transferred across boundary frequencies where a learned decoder did not |
| Fast multipole and translation operators | Far-field interactions between separated bodies are analytic expansions; only near-field is geometry-specific | Expansion order; near-field corrections for close bodies | Attention over all tokens learns near and far interactions alike from data |
| Pressure–velocity coupling (projection, SIMPLE) | The pressure solve enforces a global constraint (mass conservation) exactly at every step | A Poisson solve per step | Pressure is predicted pointwise; conservation is not enforced (the interior chapter of the program book reports pressure as a gauge quantity with no constraint) |
| Wall models and near-wall resolution | The near-wall region is modelled by a local law (log law, wall function) that is the same on every wall | Mesh grading or a modelled first cell | A uniform token budget; the audit's harmonic-disk spectrum control shows wall flux needs modes the interior does not |
| Closure models (RANS, hybrid RANS–LES) | Turbulent stresses are local algebraic or transport relations, calibrated once, applied everywhere | Model error; closure-dependent labels | The surrogate must learn the closure's imprint from labels; the eddy-viscosity gap (1.26x, program book) may be exactly this |
| Newton / Jacobian-based nonlinear solves | Local linearization gives quadratic convergence near a solution on any geometry | Jacobian assembly or its action; globalization | No state to linearize around; branch and regime are not represented (regime extrapolation fails ~10x for every architecture tested) |
| Continuation in a parameter | A solution at one condition initializes the next; branches are tracked, not extrapolated | One solve per step | Interpolation in condition space from labels; stall boundaries are not tracked |
| Mesh adaptation driven by error indicators | Resolution follows the solution's own difficulty | Indicator evaluation and remeshing | Sampling density fixed by the dataset; the program's density-robustness tests show large sensitivity in some configurations |
| Nondimensionalization and scaling | Inputs enter at unit scale by construction; conditioning is controlled | None | Left to the recipe; a dimensional freestream input produced a 2.8x artifact in this program (UDRV) |
| Conservation and compatibility enforced by construction | Fluxes balance across faces; Neumann data are compatible | Discretization design | Enforced only if the architecture is built for it; ISLA enforces symmetry contracts, not conservation |

Two patterns run through the table. First, classical solvers separate *what
is local and universal* (the operator, the closure, the wall law) from *what
is global and case-specific* (the solution), and produce the second from the
first by iteration or exact algebra at run time. Surrogates learn the global
object directly, so they must see the family they are asked about. Second,
solvers carry an error estimate in the residual, so they can spend more work
where a case is harder; surrogates spend a fixed amount everywhere and report
no uncertainty. The audit's mechanisms chapter adds the caution that a small
residual is not a small error without a stability bound, so the residual is a
control signal, not a certificate.

## Hypotheses this inventory generates {#sec-classical-hypotheses}

Each hypothesis names the ingredient it borrows, what would falsify it, and
its relation to the program's existing evidence. The order is by expected
information per unit cost.

1. **Global constraint by solve, local prediction by network** (borrowed
   from projection methods). Predict the velocity or a surface quantity
   pointwise, then obtain pressure by solving the constraint it must satisfy
   (a Poisson solve for divergence-free velocity in the interior; for a
   surface-only task, a global consistency solve is not available, which is
   itself informative about why surface pressure is the hard target).
   Falsifier: on the DrivAerML volume task, pressure from a Poisson solve of
   the predicted velocity is no more accurate than the directly predicted
   pressure. Evidence bearing on it: ISLA's interior velocity is the field it
   predicts best (0.64x GeoTransolver-volume); if the constraint solve turns
   that into a pressure advantage, the pointwise-pressure gap closes for a
   reason the mechanism names. Cost: one sparse solve per case at
   inference, no training change; can be run as an eval-only study on saved
   volume predictions if the sampled interior points support a
   discretization, otherwise on a coarse background grid with stated
   interpolation error.

2. **Wall law as an architectural prior** (borrowed from wall models). The
   program's eddy-viscosity gap and the audit's wall-flux spectrum argument
   both say the near-wall region needs resolution the interior does not. A
   surrogate that predicts wall shear through a learned local law of wall
   distance, local velocity and local pressure gradient, with the same law on
   every wall, would transfer that law across families. Falsifier: a local
   law fitted on DrivAerML does not reduce wall-shear error on the SHIFT-SUV
   fastback relative to a direct prediction. This is a component evaluation
   with target labels used only for scoring.

3. **Near-field / far-field split with analytic translation** (borrowed from
   fast multipole). The composition study (@sec-composition) tests whether
   local responses compose; the exterior variant asks whether far-field
   interactions between separated bodies can be analytic while only
   near-field maps are learned. Falsifier: on the five-sphere family, a
   truncated multipole coupling with exact local responses fails to
   reproduce the reference pressure difference the audit resolved (0.005 in
   pressure coefficient) at an order that stays fixed as bodies move apart.

4. **Residual as a control signal** (borrowed from iterative solvers). Even
   without a certificate, a residual of an available approximate operator
   (potential flow with a wake model, or a coarse RANS operator) evaluated on
   the surrogate's prediction may rank cases by difficulty and flag failures.
   Falsifier: the residual's correlation with the true per-case error is
   below 0.5 on held-out families, or no better than the model's own seed
   disagreement (which the program measured at +0.67 in-family at 35 cases
   and near zero at 1,260). The value is triage, not accuracy.

5. **Learned smoother or prolongation on a classical hierarchy** (borrowed
   from multigrid, the surviving form of the audit's fourth direction after
   @sec-solver-spaces). The coarse space stays geometric; the network learns
   the part classical methods choose heuristically (smoother weights,
   prolongation stencils) conditioned on local operator entries. Prerequisite
   gate: exhibit an operator class where the classical hierarchy degrades
   (anisotropy, high Péclet, a state-dependent Jacobian); without such a
   failure there is nothing to learn.

6. **Continuation instead of extrapolation** (borrowed from Newton and
   continuation methods). Regime extrapolation fails for every architecture
   tested; a solver would not extrapolate across stall but continue from the
   nearest solved angle. A surrogate conditioned on a nearby *solution* (the
   audit's state-conditioned extension) rather than on the condition alone is
   the learned analogue. Falsifier: conditioning on the field at the nearest
   in-distribution angle does not reduce the post-stall error below the
   unconditioned surrogate's. This needs volume or surface fields at the
   neighbouring condition at inference, which changes the product.

7. **Conservation by construction.** A surrogate whose surface pressure and
   shear integrate to forces that satisfy a momentum balance with a predicted
   wake deficit would carry a physical constraint no current model enforces.
   Falsifier: enforcing the balance as a hard or soft constraint does not
   reduce force error on held-out families. This is the weakest of the
   seven as a transfer mechanism, because the constraint is a single scalar
   relation per case.

## Priority and what runs first {#sec-classical-priority}

Hypothesis 1 was run as an eval-only study on the saved DrivAerML interior
predictions and **stops at its instrument gates** (@sec-nb-h1-verdict;
`studies/poisson_pressure/`): the 10,000 scattered interior points per car
(6 × 10⁻⁵ of the CFD mesh, neighbours 3–16 cm apart) do not resolve the
velocity field. The discrete divergence of the *true* velocity is 35% of
its gradient norm, the meshfree Laplacian misses a 1 m analytic field by
12% (median over cars) to 124% (mean), and the pressure recovered from the
true velocity by momentum least squares is off by a factor 7.7 (median)
against a bar of 0.10, so the recovered-from-predicted comparison was never
meaningful and was not graded. The same fact closes hypothesis 4 on these
artifacts: any physics residual computed on the saved samples is dominated
by the sample's own discretization error. Both hypotheses now wait on a
data-plumbing node (dense re-sampled evaluations, or the full mesh), whose
cost is the real price of "global constraint by solve" for surrogates
evaluated on sparse samples. Hypothesis 2 is a two-lane component evaluation and a
natural companion to the program's eddy-viscosity work. Hypothesis 3 rides on
the composition study's exterior variant. Hypotheses 5 through 7 are gated
on prerequisites (a failing classical hierarchy; neighbouring-condition
fields at inference; a conservation relation with predictive content) and
are recorded here so that they are not rediscovered later without their
falsifiers.
